layers.name: Terrain
layers.why: The shape of the land decides where water runs, what can be seen from where, and how much earthmoving a large flat building platform would need.

layers.name: Water
layers.why: Data centres need water for cooling and change how rain drains from a site. Rivers, burns, ponds and reservoirs show where that water would come from and go to.

layers.name: Buildings
layers.why: Footprints and heights of existing buildings give a sense of scale against which a proposed facility can be judged.

layers.name: Roads
layers.why: Roads carry construction traffic and connect a site to the places around it.

layers.name: Railways
layers.why: Working and disused railways trace earlier industries, such as coal, oil and steel. Their routes often decide where later development goes.

layers.name: Power
layers.why: Substations, high-voltage lines, battery storage and generators often explain why a site is chosen. A data centre's demand for electricity is measured in tens or hundreds of megawatts.

layers.name: Industrial residues
layers.why: Mines, bings, quarries, landfill and old works are what earlier industries left behind. They are part of the landscape, not empty land, and they can affect ground stability and contamination.

layers.name: Schools, care and community
layers.why: Schools, care homes, hospitals and community buildings are where noise, light, traffic and air quality matter most. Only the type of building is shown, never names or addresses of homes.

layers.name: Land cover
layers.why: Farmland, woodland, heath and industrial ground together describe a worked landscape, neither an idyll nor a wasteland.

layers.name: Planning allocations
layers.why: Local development plans zone land, for example as 'employment land'. Seeing those zones shows how a site came to be described as available.

layers.name: Proposed data centre
layers.why: The proposed footprint and its stated height, shown as a removable block. Its precision is stated on every export.
